passage: The fan stopped mid-turn and the room went black. "Power cut again!" Jeevan groaned from the sofa. "Where is the torch?" "Second shelf, left side, behind the biscuit tin," Rafiq said, already moving. A click, and a white circle of light wobbled on the wall. "Matches?" "Same shelf, in the little steel box. I will hand it to you, Papa, and you light the candle." "Good boy. And the hand fan?" "On the hook by the door." Rafiq waved it at his father's face. "It happens every summer, so I keep everything in one place." Jeevan laughed. "Ten minutes and we are already comfortable. Thank you, Rafiq."

qa.q: Where did Rafiq keep the torch?
qa.a: He kept the torch on the second shelf, left side, behind the biscuit tin.

qa.q: How does Rafiq feel about helping when the lights go out?
qa.a: Calm and a little proud, since he already knew where each thing was and looked after his father's comfort.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq prepare for the next power cut, and why?
qa.a: He could keep spare batteries beside the torch, because a torch is only useful if it works when the lights go.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel about the way the family handled the power cut?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, since he laughed and thanked Rafiq after ten minutes, already comfortable. 🙂

grounding: A child keeps a torch, matches and a hand fan in a known place so he can help quickly in a summer power cut.

passage: Every summer in our town, the lights go off at least twice a week, usually just when Dadi is cooking. Last year I got tired of everyone stumbling around shouting, "Where's the torch?" So I, Pradeep, took an old biscuit tin and put in the big torch, a box of matches for the grown-ups, two candles and Dadi's palm-leaf hand fan. I kept it on the shelf right next to the kitchen door, and I told everyone, even my little cousin Mahima. The next time the power went, I walked straight to the shelf in the dark, three steps from the door. In ten seconds the torch was on and Dadi had her fan. She said I was the family's electricity board. Now I check the torch batteries every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Pradeep put in the tin?
qa.a: The big torch, a box of matches for the grown-ups, two candles and Dadi's palm-leaf hand fan.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Dadi called it the family's electricity board?
qa.a: Pradeep felt proud and pleased that the plan worked.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep add to the tin?
qa.a: Spare torch batteries, so a flat battery doesn't undo the whole plan.

qa.q: What is the next power cut like for Dadi?
qa.a: Dadi gets light and her fan in ten seconds instead of waiting in the dark.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes keeping a torch, matches and a hand fan in a known place for summer power cuts.

passage:
Class 4 note, April.
After last week's power cut, when our room went dark during the drawing period and three children panicked, Madhav came to me with an idea. "Can we keep a torch in class? And the paper fans we made?" We agreed a plan together. He brought a shoebox, labelled it POWER CUT in big letters, and packed two torches from the office, the paper fans and a whistle for the class monitor. He chose the spot himself: the first shelf by the door, "so anyone can find it without looking". Today the lights went out again at noon. Before I could speak, Madhav had the torches on and was handing out fans. The class stayed calm. I have asked him to check the torch batteries every Monday.
Mehak, class teacher

qa.q: Where did Madhav keep the box?
qa.a: On the first shelf by the door.

qa.q: How did Madhav likely feel when the lights went out today?
qa.a: Calm and ready, and probably proud as he handed out the fans.

qa.q: What else could help the class in future cuts?
qa.a: A short practice, so every child knows where the box is and what to do.

qa.q: How did the class experience today's power cut?
qa.a: The class stayed calm, with torches and fans ready in moments.

grounding: A teacher's note records a child preparing a power-cut box in a known place and helping the class quickly when the lights go out.
